When users don’t know who to call: designing Bricio Anna Diyanova 8 min read · Oct 29, 2026 -- Listen Share How a friend’s story and prototype research shaped a home repair assistant Press enter or click to view image in full size Bricio: a home repair app concept connecting assistance, service selection, and visit requests. UI design by Anna Diyanova; mascot created with AI assistance. A friend told me about a leak in her mother’s bathroom. According to her account, an ageing seal in a radiator connection had started leaking onto the washing machine underneath it. Her mother was home alone and became frightened. She tried calling her children, but they were at work and could not answer immediately. At that moment, she did not know what to do next or whom to call for help. That story became the starting point for Bricio, an independent mobile app concept and interactive Figma prototype. I wanted to explore assistance before booking: helping someone understand what their next step might be, whether professional help is needed, and how urgently to seek it. I did not take this one experience as evidence that all older adults react the same way. What stayed with me was the situation: being alone with an unfamiliar problem and being unable to reach someone you trust. I wanted to explore an interface for that moment, rather than assume everyone arrives ready to choose a service. A catalog starts with an assumption A service catalog is useful when people already know what they need. Someone looking for furniture assembly can choose a category, review a specialist, and arrange a visit. But a category such as Plumbing or Appliances also asks the person to classify the problem before they have received any help. For Bricio, I treated that uncertainty as a design hypothesis worth exploring. Could the app help people describe what they can see before asking them to choose a profession? I kept two entry points on the home screen: camera-based assistance and a manual catalog. They address different starting points. One begins with an observation; the other begins with a service the person already knows they want. The assistant existed, but it was not easy enough to find In an earlier version, the AI assistant had a small icon on the home screen and also appeared in the catalog. I had made assistance available, but the research showed that availability alone was not enough. I conducted a small study with five participants using the Figma prototype. One observation was that participants initially went to the catalog and tried to find a specialist themselves. The feedback also indicated that they wanted to be able to find the assistant immediately when needed and start a conversation with it. I used these findings to inform the next iteration, not to draw conclusions about all potential users. Those observations changed the home screen. I introduced a dedicated banner with the mascot and made the central “+” action more visually prominent as an entry point to assistance. The intention was to make help visible before someone had to navigate service categories. Press enter or click to view image in full size The revised home screen gives the assistant a dedicated banner alongside the manual catalog. This image shows the revised design, not a before-and-after comparison. UI design by Anna Diyanova; mascot created with AI assistance. This was a change to the hierarchy, not the addition of another AI feature. The assistant was already part of the concept; I needed to make its role easier to discover. A familiar face for an unfamiliar situation The mascot was a product decision, not just a visual addition. Someone dealing with an unexpected problem at home may need more than a list of options: they may also need a reassuring presence and a clear explanation of what happens next. I wanted Bricio’s AI to feel less abstract, so I gave the assistant a recognizable character with a friendly face and expressive reactions. I designed its role to extend across the journey, from the first introduction and camera guidance to choosing a specialist and sending a visit request. The same character connects these moments, helping the experience feel like a continuous conversation rather than a series of unrelated screens. Its role is to explain the next step and acknowledge progress, while the person stays in control of the decisions. The cute appearance and varied expressions were intentional, too. I wanted the assistant to feel approachable and supportive, helping create a calmer, more pleasant experience during an unfamiliar task. That is an emotional design goal, not a measured outcome of the prototype study. A friendly character should support clear guidance without making uncertain AI suggestions seem more reliable than they are. The camera is the beginning of a conversation The camera scenario in the prototype is separate from the incident that inspired the project: it uses a washing machine with an error on its display and water on the floor.
